title: Job Sequencing with Deadlines
directAnswer: Each unit-time job earns its profit only if it runs at or before its deadline. Greedily process jobs from highest profit to lowest, and place each one in the LATEST free time slot at or before its deadline. Scheduling late leaves the early slots open for tighter-deadline jobs that come later. With a simple slot array the scan is O(n·maxDeadline); with disjoint-set union (path-compressed 'find the latest free slot') it's effectively O(n log n).

remember.pattern: Sort by profit desc, place each job in the latest free slot ≤ its deadline
rules: Process jobs by **profit descending** — commit to the most valuable jobs first.
Place each job as **late as possible** (latest free slot ≤ deadline), never early — this preserves earlier slots for jobs with tighter deadlines.
Jobs are **unit time**: each occupies exactly one integer slot, so feasibility is purely 'is there a free slot ≤ deadline?'.
Slots are 1-indexed up to maxDeadline; a job with deadline d can use any of slots 1..d.
For speed, replace the inner backward scan with union-find where find(d) jumps straight to the latest free slot ≤ d, then unions it to d−1.
whenToUse: Unit-time jobs, each with a deadline and a profit; maximise total profit of on-time jobs
A single machine processing one job per time unit
You can drop jobs entirely (no partial credit) and order is free within deadlines
Classic 'sort by value, fit greedily into latest slot' scheduling
antiSignals: Jobs have arbitrary (non-unit) durations → this greedy breaks; use DP / flow
You must run every job (no dropping) → feasibility/ordering problem, not selection
Objective is minimise lateness / weighted completion time → different scheduling theory
Multiple machines in parallel → load-balancing, not single-slot greedy
remember.takeaway: Two greedy decisions combine here: take the most profitable jobs first (so a forced drop sacrifices the cheapest job), and schedule each as late as its deadline allows (so early slots stay open for urgent jobs). The latest-free-slot lookup is the textbook use of union-find as a 'next available pointer', turning an O(n·D) scan into near-linear time.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you combine TWO greedy ideas — sort by profit descending AND place each job in the latest free slot before its deadline — and can argue why scheduling late is what makes it optimal.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Placing jobs in the EARLIEST free slot (which needlessly blocks urgent jobs), or sorting by deadline instead of profit, or forgetting that jobs are unit-time.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain the exchange argument: filling the latest slot never hurts a future job that an earlier slot could have served, and processing high-profit first means any unavoidable drop removes the least valuable job. Then upgrade the O(n·D) slot scan to union-find for near-linear time.

problemStatement:
You are given `n` jobs. Each job `i` has a **deadline** `deadline[i]` and a **profit** `profit[i]`, and takes exactly **one unit of time** to run. A single machine runs one job per time unit, starting at time 1.

A job earns its profit only if it is scheduled to finish at or before its deadline. Choose a subset and an ordering that **maximises the total profit** of on-time jobs. Return the number of jobs done and the total profit (or just the maximum profit).
constraints: 1 ≤ deadline[i] ≤ n (a deadline beyond n is never more useful than n)
1 ≤ profit[i] ≤ 10⁹ (sum can exceed a 32-bit int → accumulate profit in a long)
Each job is unit time and can be dropped if it can't be scheduled on time
understanding: Time is divided into unit slots 1, 2, 3, …. Each job needs one slot no later than its deadline. We're choosing which jobs to run and when, to maximise profit. Since every job takes the same time, the only thing that distinguishes them is profit and how tight their deadline is — so we prioritise profit and use deadlines only to decide whether a slot is still available.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does every job take the same amount of time?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — unit time. That's the assumption that makes the greedy correct; arbitrary durations would need DP or flow.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I skip jobs that can't be scheduled on time?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. We maximise profit over the jobs we *can* fit; an unschedulable job simply earns nothing.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can total profit overflow a 32-bit integer?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: With up to 10⁵ jobs at 10⁹ each, the sum reaches 10¹⁴ — well past int range. I accumulate in a long.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are deadlines bounded by n?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Effectively yes — a deadline larger than n can't help since there are at most n slots worth using. I cap maxDeadline at n.

approaches.name: Sort by Profit + Slot Array (Baseline-to-Solid)
approaches.whenToMention: Start here: it's the clear, correct greedy. State its O(n·maxDeadline) cost, then offer union-find to speed the slot lookup.
hints: Every job is the same length, so the only reasons to prefer one over another are its profit and how soon it's due. Which should drive the order you consider jobs?
Sort jobs by profit descending. For each job, you want to run it as LATE as possible without missing its deadline. Why late and not early?
Keep a boolean slot array of size maxDeadline. For the current job, scan from its deadline downward to slot 1 and grab the first free slot; if none, drop the job.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting is O(n log n). For each of the n jobs, the backward scan for a free slot costs up to maxDeadline in the worst case, giving O(n·maxDeadline). The slot array is O(maxDeadline) space.
approaches.explanation:
Sort jobs by profit, highest first. Maintain `slot[1..maxDeadline]`, all free. For each job, search from `min(maxDeadline, deadline)` down to 1 for a free slot; if you find one, occupy it and bank the profit, otherwise drop the job.

**Why sort by profit descending.** If a slot conflict ever forces us to drop a job, we want the dropped job to be the *least* valuable one. Considering jobs from most to least profitable guarantees that whenever we're forced to skip, every job already placed is at least as valuable — so the loss is minimised. This is the 'most valuable first' half of the greedy.

**Why place each job in the LATEST free slot, not the earliest.** This is the subtle, decisive choice. A job with deadline d can run in any slot 1..d. If we put it in the earliest free slot, we consume an early slot that a *later-considered, tighter-deadline* job might desperately need (that urgent job can only use early slots). By placing the current job as late as its deadline permits, we keep the early slots open as long as possible. Filling from the back never costs us anything: any future job that could have used the slot we took could equally use an earlier still-free slot, because that future job's deadline is ≥ the slot we filled. This is the exchange argument — swapping a late placement for an earlier one never increases the number of feasible jobs.

**Why unit time is essential.** Because each job occupies exactly one slot, feasibility reduces to 'is any slot ≤ deadline free?'. There's no packing of variable lengths, no fragmentation — that clean structure is precisely what lets the greedy be optimal. Drop the unit-time assumption and the argument collapses; you'd need DP or flow.

**The cost wrinkle.** The backward scan per job can walk up to maxDeadline slots, so a worst case (many jobs with large deadlines all colliding) is O(n·maxDeadline). That's fine for moderate inputs, but the next approach removes it.
approaches.insight: Two greedy choices stack: profit-descending order means any forced drop sacrifices the cheapest job, and latest-slot placement means a placement never steals a slot a tighter-deadline job uniquely needs. The latest-slot rule is the non-obvious one — most people reach for the earliest slot and quietly lose optimality.

code.python:
def job_scheduling(self, deadline: list[int], profit: list[int]) -> tuple[int, int]:
    n = len(deadline)
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: profit[i], reverse=True)  # profit desc
    max_d = max(deadline)
    slot = [False] * (max_d + 1)  # 1-indexed
    count = 0
    total_profit = 0
    for i in order:
        for t in range(min(max_d, deadline[i]), 0, -1):
            if not slot[t]:
                slot[t] = True
                count += 1
                total_profit += profit[i]
                break
    return count, total_profit

approaches.name: Profit Sort + Union-Find Slot Lookup (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Bring this up after the slot-array version to kill the O(n·maxDeadline) worst case — phrase it as 'union-find as a next-free-slot pointer'.
hints: The slow part of the slot-array version is the backward scan for a free slot. Could you jump straight to the latest free slot ≤ d in almost O(1)?
Use a disjoint-set structure where parent[t] points to the latest free slot at or before t. find(d) returns it directly.
After assigning slot t, union it to t−1 so future finds skip past the now-occupied slot. Path compression makes this near-constant amortised.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting is O(n log n). Each job does one find (and one union), each near-O(α(n)) ≈ O(1) amortised with path compression, so the scheduling phase is effectively O(n·α(n)). Space is O(maxDeadline) for the parent array.
approaches.explanation:
Keep the same two greedy decisions — profit-descending order, latest-slot placement — but replace the linear backward scan with a disjoint-set union (DSU) that answers 'what's the latest free slot ≤ d?' in near-constant time.

**The DSU-as-pointer idea.** Initialise `parent[t] = t` for t in 0..maxDeadline. The invariant is: `find(t)` returns the largest still-free slot index that is ≤ t (or 0 if none remain). For a job with deadline d, call `find(d)`. If it returns a slot s ≥ 1, that slot is free — assign the job there, bank the profit, and then `union(s, s−1)` by setting `parent[s] = s − 1`. That union makes every future `find` that lands on s skip down to the latest free slot below s. Path compression flattens the chains so repeated finds are amortised near O(1).

**Why this preserves correctness.** The greedy logic is unchanged: we still take jobs most-profitable-first and still place each in the latest free slot ≤ its deadline — the exchange argument from the slot-array approach applies verbatim. DSU only changes *how fast* we locate that latest free slot; it never changes *which* slot we pick. `find(d)` returns exactly the slot the backward scan would have found (the highest free index ≤ d), and pointing s to s−1 after use is just an O(1) way to mark s occupied and remember where the next free slot is.

**Why the speed-up matters.** The slot-array scan is O(n·maxDeadline) in the worst case — pathological when many jobs share large deadlines and collide. DSU collapses each lookup to amortised α(n) (the inverse Ackermann function, ≤ 4 for any realistic n), so the whole scheduling phase is effectively linear and the algorithm is dominated by the initial O(n log n) sort.

**Slot 0 as the sentinel.** Index 0 represents 'no free slot available'. When `find(d)` returns 0, every slot ≤ d is taken and the job is dropped. Unioning the last used slot down toward 0 naturally funnels exhausted deadlines to this sentinel.
approaches.insight: Union-find shines as a 'next available resource' pointer: each slot, once used, forwards future queries to the next free slot below it. This 'point to the previous free index' trick recurs in problems like painting/booking intervals and 'smallest available id'. The greedy proof is identical to the slot-array version — DSU is purely an accelerator for the latest-free-slot query.

code.python:
def job_scheduling(self, deadline: list[int], profit: list[int]) -> tuple[int, int]:
    n = len(deadline)
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: profit[i], reverse=True)  # profit desc
    max_d = max(deadline)
    parent = list(range(max_d + 1))  # slot 0 = sentinel

    def find(x: int) -> int:
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]  # path halving
            x = parent[x]
        return x

    count = 0
    total_profit = 0
    for i in order:
        slot = find(min(max_d, deadline[i]))
        if slot > 0:
            parent[slot] = slot - 1  # mark used, forward to previous free
            count += 1
            total_profit += profit[i]
    return count, total_profit

java.explanation: Path compression — flattens the chain so repeated finds are near O(1).

pitfalls: Forgetting the slot-0 sentinel — find could return an invalid slot and you'd schedule a job nowhere.
Skipping path compression — finds degrade toward O(maxDeadline) and you lose the speed-up.
Unioning to slot+1 instead of slot−1 — you must forward to the EARLIER free slot, not later.
Capping deadline incorrectly — clamp to maxDeadline so find stays in bounds.

edgeCases.behavior: find(1) succeeds once, then parent[1]=0 → every later job finds slot 0 and is dropped.
Each find hits a fresh slot → all jobs scheduled.
Tie order doesn't affect total profit; both get distinct slots if available.

commonMistakes: Placing each job in the earliest free slot instead of the latest — blocks tighter-deadline jobs.
Sorting by deadline rather than by profit descending.
Accumulating total profit in a 32-bit int — overflows for large inputs.
Forgetting jobs are unit-time and trying to pack arbitrary durations with the same greedy.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Earliest-slot instead of latest-slot placement
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Filling early slots consumes capacity that tight-deadline jobs (considered later) uniquely need. Placing each job as late as its deadline allows keeps early slots open and is what makes the greedy optimal.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Sorting by deadline rather than profit
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Deadline order can place a low-profit job into a slot a high-profit job needed, reducing total profit. Profit-descending order guarantees any forced drop is the least valuable job.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Profit accumulated in int
commonMistakesDetailed.why: With up to 10⁵ jobs at 10⁹ profit each, the total reaches ~10¹⁴ and overflows a 32-bit int silently. Use a long (Java) — Python ints are unbounded.

patternNote: Canonical 'value-first greedy + latest-free-slot' scheduling. Sort by profit descending, schedule each unit job as late as its deadline allows, and use union-find as a next-free-slot pointer for near-linear time. The DSU 'point to previous free index' trick reappears in interval booking and smallest-available-id problems.
